passage:
At nine, Chetan struggled through a page of his reader while classmates waited. That evening he dropped it on the floor. "I'm just lazy," he told his mother. "I'll never be good at reading." For weeks he stopped trying, and the word "lazy" sat over every homework hour like a lid.

At twenty, Chetan shared a hostel flat with two very different roommates. Jasleen changed her plans on a whim, tried every cuisine and spent Sundays at strangers' concerts. Minakshi kept the same routine each morning, called her grandmother every evening and preferred old songs to new ones. Their friends had already stuck labels on them: "shallow" and "boring".

Chetan remembered how one word had once flattened him. Instead of picking a side, he asked Jasleen what she loved about surprises, then asked Minakshi what her routines gave her. Jasleen said, "It makes me feel alive." Minakshi said, "It keeps me calm." Chetan nodded. They ended up cooking together, and each taught him something.

qa.q: What did Chetan say about himself after struggling with the reader at nine?
qa.a: Chetan said he was just lazy and would never be good at reading.

qa.q: How does the label Chetan gave himself at nine connect to the way he treats Jasleen and Minakshi at twenty?
qa.a: At nine the word lazy replaced a specific skill and made him stop trying, and at twenty he sees how labels like shallow and boring flatten people, so he asks what each style protects and avoids labelling curiosity as shallow or caution as dull.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he dropped the reader and called himself lazy?
qa.a: Chetan felt discouraged and ashamed about his slow reading, so he gave up rather than practise.

qa.q: What did Chetan do that showed respect for both roommates?
qa.a: He asked Jasleen what she loved about surprises and Minakshi what her routines gave her, listening without picking a side.

grounding: Labelling and respect for different styles: a child who calls himself lazy, and the same person later declining to label an open roommate as shallow or a traditional one as boring.

passage:
When Preeti's admission letter to the top engineering college arrived, her whole street celebrated. Preeti smiled and thought, "They must have made a mistake." In her first year she looked at classmates who seemed to understand everything at once and told herself she was a fraud who had slipped through by luck. Her friend Farhan said, "You cleared the same exam I did." She shrugged, unconvinced.

Five years later, in her first job, the same worry surfaced whenever a review approached. This time Preeti kept a folder called "Proof". In it she saved the list of tasks she had finished, a thank-you note from a client and the line from her manager Hrithik: "Your fix saved us two days."

Before a big presentation she felt her doubt rise, sat down and read the folder slowly. The evidence stood there in plain words. She still felt nervous, but she walked in with the folder in her mind, and it steadied her.

qa.q: What did Preeti call the folder where she kept her evidence?
qa.a: She called the folder "Proof".

qa.q: How does Preeti's thought in her first year connect with the folder she keeps at work?
qa.a: In her first year Preeti believed she was a fraud who got in by luck, and later the same doubt returns, but she tests it against facts in her Proof folder instead of trying to feel confident.

qa.q: What was Preeti probably feeling when she thought they must have made a mistake?
qa.a: Preeti felt unworthy and afraid of being found out, so she discounted her success and compared herself harshly with classmates.

qa.q: Why does reading the folder help Preeti before a presentation?
qa.a: It sets plain evidence of her completed work and praise against the thought that she is a fraud, so she can face the presentation even while nervous.

grounding: Imposter feelings: a student who believes she got into a top college by luck, and the same person later testing that thought against a written record of her work.

passage:
Nine-year-old Eshaan's mother Sangeeta only ever asked, "What was your score?" When a test paper came home with a mistake, she went quiet, and Eshaan learned to say, "It was easy," and slide the paper away. He came to believe that a cross in red ink meant less love in the house.

At twenty, Eshaan was stuck on a college essay. His friend Rashmi watched him rewrite the opening for the fourth time. "Set a timer for forty minutes," she suggested. "Write the whole rough thing first. Ask yourself what would happen if it landed at ninety percent of your hope." Eshaan felt his chest tighten. He wrote a clumsy draft anyway, and it was awkward and uneven. Rashmi read it and pointed at two lines that were good.

He edited it for another hour, then sent it. "It's not perfect," he said. "But it exists." When he noticed the old tightness returning before the next essay, he booked a talk at the student counselling centre.

qa.q: How long did Rashmi suggest that Eshaan set the timer for?
qa.a: Rashmi suggested forty minutes.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta's question about scores in Eshaan's childhood connect to Rashmi's advice at twenty?
qa.a: Sangeeta responds only to marks, so Eshaan learns that love depends on being flawless and hides mistakes; Rashmi's timer, rough first draft and ninety-percent question give him practice in tolerating small imperfection, which loosens that old belief.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling as he slid his marked paper away at nine?
qa.a: Eshaan felt anxious and ashamed of his mistake, afraid it meant less love.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan book a talk at the counselling centre?
qa.a: The old tightness kept coming back, and persistent anxiety deserves support from someone trained to help, not only tips from a friend.

grounding: Perfectionism from a child feeling loved only for marks, to a young adult practising good enough with a time limit and a rough first version.

passage:
At five, Tushar hid behind his mother Usha's legs at a wedding, ignoring every greeting. Usha did not tell him to be brave. She stood close, a warm hand on his head, and after a while he stepped out to look at the drums.

At fifteen, Tushar snapped at his classmate Devika in the corridor: "You always ruin group work." Devika went pale and walked away. For three days Tushar replayed the moment over and over: her face, his tone, the word "always". He told himself that being hard on himself was the honest thing to do, but it mostly made him feel ashamed. He took the long way round the school so he would not meet her, and began finding reasons to stay home.

On the fourth evening Usha sat near him on the balcony and did not ask questions. "You're carrying something," she said. Tushar told her. The next morning he found Devika at her locker and said, "I was unfair. I'm sorry." She nodded slowly.

qa.q: What did Tushar step out to look at at the wedding?
qa.a: Tushar stepped out to look at the drums.

qa.q: How is Tushar's behaviour at fifteen like hiding behind his mother at five, and how do the ways out compare?
qa.a: At five he hides behind his mother, and at fifteen he takes the long way round school and stays home to avoid Devika, both because staying away from the scary thing feels like relief; in both cases Usha's calm nearness, not pushing, brings him out.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling as he replayed the corridor moment for three days?
qa.a: Tushar felt ashamed and worried, and his harsh self-review kept him stuck instead of helping him repair things.

qa.q: What did Usha do that helped Tushar face Devika?
qa.a: Usha sat near him without questioning, said he was carrying something, and listened, which gave him the courage to apologise the next day.

grounding: Avoidance and rumination: a child hiding behind a parent at a wedding, and a teenager replaying a harsh remark and avoiding the classmate until a parent's calm nearness helps him face it.

passage:
At five, Parul stood with her arms wrapped around her father Akash's leg at a neighbour's party. Every time a grown-up said hello she buried her face in his trousers. Akash did not pull her away. He said, "We'll just watch the games together," and soon she was giggling from behind him at the dancing balloons.

At nine, Parul had a quarrel with her best friend about a borrowed pencil case and got a low mark in maths the same week. Every evening her mother Deepika asked, "How was school?" and Parul said, "Fine." The quarrel and the mark sat in her chest like stones, and by Thursday she felt sick at dinner.

Deepika noticed her pushing the rice around her plate. She put her fork down and spoke gently. "Whatever it is, we can look at it together. It won't be a big scene." Parul took a breath, pulled out the maths paper and told her everything, starting with the pencil case.

qa.q: What was Parul's quarrel with her best friend about?
qa.a: The quarrel was about a borrowed pencil case.

qa.q: How is Parul's behaviour at the party like her silence at dinner four years later?
qa.a: At the party Parul hides behind her father to avoid the scary greetings, and at nine she hides the quarrel and the low mark by saying fine; both feel like relief but the problem grows, and a calm parent close by makes it easier to face.

qa.q: What was Parul probably feeling as she pushed the rice around her plate on Thursday?
qa.a: Parul was worried and uneasy, with the quarrel and the low mark weighing on her like stones.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that made it easier for Parul to speak?
qa.a: Deepika put her fork down, said gently that they could look at it together, and promised no big scene, so the first admission felt safe.

grounding: Avoidance in a young child hiding behind a parent at a party, and a school-age child avoiding telling a parent about a quarrel and a low grade until a calm parent invites the talk.

passage:
At nine, Tushar tripped on the classroom step while carrying the attendance register and slid the last two metres on his knees like a penguin. The class howled. He got up, took a bow and said, "Ta-da!" Only in the corridor did he notice his knees stinging and his cheeks burning.

At twenty, he still reached for a joke when something felt awkward. When his friend Vandana wrote, "I failed the lab exam and I'm really down," Tushar typed, "lol 😅 happens to everyone" and pressed send before thinking. Vandana looked at the two little letters for a while. Was he laughing at her? Or was he uncomfortable and unsure what to say?

She wrote back, "That 'lol' felt strange. Are you okay?" Tushar stared at the screen. "Sorry. I never know what to say when people are sad, so I make a joke," he answered. Then he called her. His friend Chetan, sitting nearby, saw him step out to take it in the stairwell.

qa.q: How did Tushar slide across the floor at nine?
qa.a: He slid the last two metres on his knees like a penguin.

qa.q: How does Tushar's clowning at nine relate to his "lol" message at twenty?
qa.a: At nine Tushar slides on his knees, takes a bow and says "Ta-da!" while his cheeks burn; at twenty he types "lol" with an emoji to Vandana, who wonders whether he is laughing at her or is uncomfortable. Both times a joke covers discomfort, and a lol could mean humour, politeness or unease.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he typed lol to Vandana's message about failing?
qa.a: Tushar felt uncomfortable and unsure what to say, so he reached for a joke.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that helped clear up the misreading?
qa.a: Vandana told Tushar the lol felt strange and asked if he was okay, which gave him the chance to explain and to call her.

grounding: Humour covering embarrassment in a child, and a young adult's lol in a text that could signal amusement, politeness or discomfort until a friend asks.
